title: Pelvic floor exercises
intro: The pelvic floor is a sling of muscles supporting the bladder, bowel and womb. Strengthening it can reduce urine leakage, improve bladder and bowel control, and support recovery after childbirth or surgery. It is easy to learn but needs regular practice for several months to see lasting results.

sections.heading: What the pelvic floor does
paragraphs: These muscles help close the openings of the bladder and bowel, support the pelvic organs and contribute to sexual function. They can be weakened by pregnancy and childbirth, menopause, chronic coughing, constipation and straining, heavy lifting, being overweight, age and some operations such as prostate surgery.

sections.heading: Finding the muscles
paragraphs: Imagine you are trying to stop passing wind and also to stop the flow of urine. The muscles you tighten are the pelvic floor. You should feel a lift and squeeze inside while the buttocks, thighs and abdomen stay relaxed, and you should keep breathing. Do not practise by stopping urine midstream regularly, as this can disturb bladder emptying.

sections.heading: How to do the exercises
paragraphs: Squeeze and lift the muscles, hold for a few seconds, then release fully for the same amount of time. Build up to holding for about ten seconds, ten repetitions, several times a day. Also practise quick contractions. Use the muscles before coughing, sneezing or lifting. Link the exercises to daily routines such as brushing teeth.

sections.heading: Getting guidance
paragraphs: Many people do the exercises incorrectly, for example by pushing down or holding their breath. A physiotherapist or specialist nurse can check your technique and design a programme, and may use biofeedback or devices. Training in a group or with an app can help motivation.

sections.heading: Who benefits
paragraphs: Exercises help with stress incontinence, urgency, mild prolapse, postnatal recovery and after prostate surgery, and may help sexual function. Improvement usually takes weeks to months, and regular continuation is needed. Seek advice if you cannot feel the muscles, have pain, or if symptoms do not improve.

examples.title: Building a habit
examples.text: Imagine you leak urine when you cough. You could do a set of exercises after each toilet visit and while waiting for the kettle, and keep a record for three months.

examples.title: Checking your technique
examples.text: Suppose you are unsure whether you are doing them correctly. You might ask a physiotherapist to examine you and give feedback.
